transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-05
Start time: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Michael Ortiz (FinLedger CTO), Sara Lopez (Head of MLOps), Evan Park (SRE), Janelle Kim (Product)

Summary:
Quick scoping call to align on POC success criteria and to size workload for benchmarking. Main focus: QPS, concurrency, input/output token distribution, and timeline for a 1-week pilot.

Topics: Workload characterization, test harness, synthetic vs replayed traffic, latency SLOs, capacity (dedicated vs hosted), security considerations (KMS/SAML/SOC2), and next steps for scheduling pilot.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, uh thanks for joining. I'm Alex from Redwood, AE on the account, Priya our SE is here, hi Priya.
[00:07] Priya: Hey, hi folks, thanks for making the time.
[00:10] Michael: Good, yeah thanks. We've been excited to, you know, get into the POC details.
[00:15] Alex: Quick agenda: sync on current traffic, define success criteria, collect traces/prompts, and agree on pilot timeline. Does that work?
[00:20] Sara: Yep, sounds good.
[00:22] Janelle: Yes.
[00:25] Alex: Cool. To start - can you give a quick overview of the production flows you're looking to move? QPS, average request size, any 95th/99th token counts?
[00:30] Michael: Sure. So we have two main call paths - ledger-query which is low latency, about 25 QPS steady with spikes to 80, and document-summarize which is heavier - approx 6 QPS steady with bursts to 20.
[00:42] Michael: Inputs for ledger-query are short, like 8-40 tokens typically, outputs 20-60 tokens. Summarize is usually 800-1,200 input tokens and outputs 100-300 tokens.
[00:50] Priya: Got it. So for the ledger path that's a high QPS but low token per call, summarize is low QPS but high tokens. That has big implications for batching and KV cache behavior.
[01:00] Evan: Also note we have ~200 concurrent users hitting the ledger-query endpoint, but only about 6 concurrent summarization jobs.
[01:06] Sara: And we prioritize p99 latency on ledger-query at <120ms if possible, summarize can be okay at p95 < 2.5s.
[01:14] Alex: Important. For the POC we should capture both 95/99 tail latency and cost per 1M tokens. Priya, what instrumentation will you need?
[01:20] Priya: We'll ask for a sample traffic trace — ideally a 72-hour replay with per-request timestamps and the raw prompt lengths. If that's not possible, a stratified sample of 10k requests with percentiles and avg tokens works. Also want a couple of representative long documents for summarize.
[01:32] Michael: We can share that, will need to anonymize account ids.
[01:35] Alex: Great. For sizing, do you have an existing RPS distribution by hour? If not, an expected peak QPS and steady QPS suffices.
[01:42] Michael: Peak ledger-query 80 QPS, steady 25. Summarize peak 20, steady 6. Spike patterns are short, 5-10 minute windows.
[01:50] Priya: That suggests for a hosted test we can provision to handle 100 QPS for ledger-query with auto-burst. For dedicated we would want to target baseline of 40-50 to keep headroom. We'll propose both configs in the model matrix.
[02:05] Alex: On benchmarks — we usually do a replay pilot where we run your trace against a few model variants and capture token/sec, latency p50/p95/p99, throughput, and pipeline cost. We'll provide a spreadsheet.
[02:15] Michael: Ok, and what about concurrency? How much does concurrency affect latency for long-form summarize?
[02:20] Priya: For long sequences concurrency isn't the main limiter, memory/KV cache and sequence length drive per-token throughput. Concurrency matters for overall QPS - for summarization if you run 6 concurrent 1k token requests, you'll see throughput drop per second because of competing GPU memory.
[02:33] Evan: We're running on GCP with a V-P-C and strict egress limits. Any special net requirements?
[02:38] Alex: We can run hosted but if you need VPC peering or Private deployment that's doable; for the POC hosted is simpler. We'll note the egress in the spreadsheet.
[02:45] Michael: For success criteria — we need ledger-query p99 < 120ms and cost per 1k tokens under $0.XX (we'll share target), plus no dropped requests during spike windows. For summarize we need acceptable quality and p95 < 2.5s.
[02:58] Alex: Perfect. We'll capture those as the POC success criteria. Priya, are there model recommendations to hit both latency and quality?
[03:05] Priya: We'll test a set: smaller optimized model for ledger-query (e.g., 7B quantized) and larger for summarize (33B float16 or 13B quantized depending on quality). We'll also try quantization profiles - 4-bit vs int8-ish, and measure delta in quality. We'll include an A/B eval metric on a small prompt set.
[03:25] Janelle: How do we handle evals? We need reproducible scoring so PMs can sign off on quality regressions.
[03:30] Priya: We'll run a small eval harness: BLEU/ROUGE-ish plus human-annotated quality on 50 cases from your QA team. We'll present a simple spreadsheet with scores.
[03:40] Michael: Timeline — looking to decide by end of March. We're flexible to run the POC the week of 3/17.
[03:45] Alex: That aligns. We'll aim to deliver the benchmark harness and propose times for a 2-hour test run.
[03:50] Evan: One concern: our security team will want SOC2 + KMS integration for keys. Is that painful in a POC?
[03:55] Alex: Not at all. For POC we can do an ephemeral test with notes on KMS; we'll share the security pack. For Private deployment it's full KMS/HSM and audit logs, but for hosted POC we provide encryption-in-transit and optional customer-managed keys if needed.
[04:10] Michael: Can you also show us cost deltas with batching and cache enabled? We want to see real cost/latency tradeoffs.
[04:16] Priya: Yes, we'll run with and without prefix/KV caching and with different batch sizes. For ledger-query, caching can reduce token computations a lot if you have repeated prefixes. We'll measure token-savings and latency impact.
[04:26] Alex: On instrumentation for benchmarks: we'll capture tokens in/out, compute time per token, GPU utilization, memory, and network egress. We'll send a template spreadsheet with columns you can fill.
[04:35] Michael: Good. For the model matrix, do you need hardware preferences? We're currently considering NVIDIA A10 vs A100 in our infra.
[04:42] Priya: For hosted tests we'll run on A100 and optionally A10 for cost comparisons. We'll note kernel differences; some models are optimized better on specific cards. We'll also capture model compilation parameters.
[04:55] Sara: Any chance we can get an estimated run time for the 72-hour trace? I mean how long will Redwood need to run it?
[05:02] Priya: If we replay full 72 hours at production speed it takes 72 hours, but we typically accelerate the replay so the wall time is shorter — we can do a compressed replay to complete in a few hours while preserving inter-request spacing strategy. We'll document burstiness so tail latencies are realistic.
[05:18] Michael: Ok sounds good. A couple of questions from our SRE: what failure modes do you typically see during a pilot?
[05:25] Alex: Most are configuration issues — batch size too big, memory OOM, or missing KV cache warmup. We'll run a small smoke test first. Also we'll set fallback to a smaller model on capacity issues.
[05:35] Evan: Alright. On the legal side — procurement asked for an initial statement of work. Is that needed to start the POC?
[05:40] Alex: For a standard hosted pilot we can start with a one-page SOW and an MSA is optional depending on data sensitivity. We'll provide a template.
[05:48] Janelle: Great. Anything else on measurement?
[05:50] Priya: We'll also capture percentiles on token generation steps  - p50/p95/p99 tokens/sec - that helps reason about long-form summarize.
[05:58] Michael: Does Redwood provide cost estimates for different quantization profiles?
[06:02] Priya: Yes, in the spreadsheet we'll include estimated cost per 1M tokens for each model/config, plus latency tradeoffs.
[06:10] Alex: Ok to recap: Alex sends benchmark spreadsheet and security pack; Priya sends model matrix and suggested test configs; FinLedger to send anonymized traffic trace and prompt samples; Redwood and FinLedger to schedule accelerated replay pilot week of 3/17. Any objections?
[06:24] Michael: No objections.
[06:26] Sara: Sounds right.
[06:28] Alex: Cool. Let's just capture success criteria explicitly in the notes: ledger-query p99 < 120ms; summarize p95 < 2.5s; cost per 1M tokens below target (FinLedger to provide target); no more than 1% error/drop during spike windows.
[06:45] Michael: Yep. Also include quality threshold — human score >= 4/5 on our sample set.
[06:50] Priya: We'll add that to the eval section.
[06:55] Alex: A couple of small clarifications... sometimes transcription picks up "KV cash" instead of KV cache so in the notes we'll write KV cache.
[07:02] Michael: (laughs) yeah the transcripts always do that.
[07:05] Priya: One more item - we'll propose two pilot modes: 1) hosted accelerated replay; 2) short dedicated node run if you want exact production fidelity. Option 2 takes ~48 hours to provision.
[07:18] Evan: Provisioning time OK. If we go with dedicated we'll need a follow-up on network peering.
[07:23] Alex: We'll handle that.
[07:25] Janelle: Next steps and owners?
[07:28] Alex: I'll send the benchmark spreadsheet and the security summary by Friday (2025-03-07). Priya you'll send model matrix by Monday (2025-03-09). FinLedger to send traces by 3/10. Then we'll lock pilot slot for 3/17.
[07:40] Michael: Confirmed.
[07:42] Alex: Anything else?
[07:43] Sara: Not from me.
[07:44] Alex: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with links — benchmark sheet, test harness repo (link: https://redwood-internal.example/bench-harness — placeholder), and security pack (link: https://redwood-docs.example/security-pack.pdf).
[07:58] Michael: Thanks, talk soon.
[08:00] Alex: Bye!
